claim: GTPase signal transduction pathways control cellular decision making by integrating multiple cellular events into a single signal.
source: GTPase signal transduction pathways control cellular decision making by integrating multiple cellular events into a single signal.
evidence: This is a general statement about GTPase pathways presented in the abstract, drawing on established scientific knowledge about signal transduction.

claim: The Mitotic Exit Network (MEN) is a Ras-like GTPase signaling pathway.
source: The Mitotic Exit Network (MEN), a Ras-like GTPase signaling pathway, integrates spatial and temporal cues to ensure that cytokinesis only occurs after the genome has partitioned between mother and daughter cells during anaphase.
evidence: This is a characterization of the MEN pathway based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The MEN integrates spatial and temporal cues to ensure that cytokinesis only occurs after the genome has partitioned between mother and daughter cells during anaphase.
source: The Mitotic Exit Network (MEN), a Ras-like GTPase signaling pathway, integrates spatial and temporal cues to ensure that cytokinesis only occurs after the genome has partitioned between mother and daughter cells during anaphase.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Signal integration in the MEN does not occur at a single step of the pathway.
source: Here we show that signal integration does not occur at a single step of the pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing regulation at multiple pathway components.

claim: Sequential components of the MEN pathway are controlled in series by different signals.
source: Rather, sequential components of the pathway are controlled in series by different signals.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing differential regulation of Tem1 and downstream kinases.

claim: The spatial signal, nuclear position, regulates the MEN GTPase Tem1.
source: The spatial signal, nuclear position, regulates the MEN GTPase Tem1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and previous literature on the zone model of MEN regulation.

claim: The temporal signal, commencement of anaphase, is mediated by mitotic cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) phosphorylation of the GTPase's downstream kinases.
source: The temporal signal, commencement of anaphase, is mediated by mitotic cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) phosphorylation of the GTPase's downstream kinases.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing CDK phosphorylation of Cdc15 and Mob1.

claim: Integrating multiple signals through sequential steps in the GTPase pathway represents a generalizable principle in GTPase signaling.
source: We propose that integrating multiple signals through sequential steps in the GTPase pathway represents a generalizable principle in GTPase signaling and explains why intracellular signal transmission is a multi-step process.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings in the MEN pathway.

claim: Serial signal integration rather than signal amplification makes multi-step signal transduction necessary.
source: Serial signal integration rather than signal amplification makes multi-step signal transduction necessary.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Accurate chromosome segregation is essential for genome maintenance and viability of the organism.
source: Accurate chromosome segregation is essential for genome maintenance and viability of the organism.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) drive progression through the cell cycle in eukaryotes.
source: In eukaryotes, a family of protein kinases, known as cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) drive progression through the cell cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Morgan, 1997.

claim: G1 CDKs promote cell cycle entry.
source: G1 CDKs promote cell cycle entry, S phase CDKs initiate DNA replication, and mitotic CDKs drive entry into mitosis (reviewed in Morgan, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: S phase CDKs initiate DNA replication.
source: G1 CDKs promote cell cycle entry, S phase CDKs initiate DNA replication, and mitotic CDKs drive entry into mitosis (reviewed in Morgan, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mitotic CDKs drive entry into mitosis.
source: G1 CDKs promote cell cycle entry, S phase CDKs initiate DNA replication, and mitotic CDKs drive entry into mitosis (reviewed in Morgan, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Events during mitosis are controlled by a ubiquitin ligase known as the Anaphase Promoting Complex or Cyclosome (APC/C).
source: Events during mitosis are controlled by a ubiquitin ligase known as the Anaphase Promoting Complex or Cyclosome (APC/C; Figure 1A; reviewed in Peters, 2006; Thornton and Toczyski, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The APC/C together with its specificity factor Cdc20 degrade the anaphase inhibitor Securin (Pds1 in budding yeast).
source: The APC/C together with its specificity factor Cdc20 degrade the anaphase inhibitor Securin (Pds1 in budding yeast; Shirayama et al., 1999), to allow the protease Separase (Esp1 in budding yeast) to cleave cohesins, the proteins that hold the duplicated sister chromatids together.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Shirayama et al., 1999.

claim: Separase (Esp1 in budding yeast) cleaves cohesins, the proteins that hold the duplicated sister chromatids together.
source: The APC/C together with its specificity factor Cdc20 degrade the anaphase inhibitor Securin (Pds1 in budding yeast; Shirayama et al., 1999), to allow the protease Separase (Esp1 in budding yeast) to cleave cohesins, the proteins that hold the duplicated sister chromatids together.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cleavage of cohesins initiates anaphase.
source: Cleavage of cohesins initiates anaphase.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell cycle biology.

claim: APC/C-Cdc20 ubiquitinylates S phase and mitotic cyclins.
source: APC/C-Cdc20 not only targets Securin for degradation, the ubiquitin ligase also ubiquitinylates S phase and mitotic cyclins (Irniger et al., 1995; King et al., 1995; Sudakin et al., 1995; Tugendreich et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In budding yeast, APC/C-Cdc20 promotes the complete destruction of the S phase cyclin Clb5.
source: In budding yeast, APC/C-Cdc20 promotes the complete destruction of the S phase cyclin Clb5 and degradation of approximately half the pool of the mitotic cyclin Clb2 (Shirayama et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Shirayama et al., 1999.

claim: In budding yeast, APC/C-Cdc20 promotes degradation of approximately half the pool of the mitotic cyclin Clb2.
source: In budding yeast, APC/C-Cdc20 promotes the complete destruction of the S phase cyclin Clb5 and degradation of approximately half the pool of the mitotic cyclin Clb2 (Shirayama et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Shirayama et al., 1999.

claim: Partial degradation of cyclins is a prerequisite for execution of the final cell cycle transition – exit from mitosis.
source: This partial degradation of cyclins is a prerequisite for execution of the final cell cycle transition – exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited literature.

claim: During exit from mitosis, the mitotic spindle is disassembled.
source: During exit from mitosis mitotic events are reversed. The mitotic spindle is disassembled, chromosomes decondense and cytokinesis ensues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitotic exit.

claim: During exit from mitosis, chromosomes decondense.
source: During exit from mitosis mitotic events are reversed. The mitotic spindle is disassembled, chromosomes decondense and cytokinesis ensues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitotic exit.

claim: During exit from mitosis, cytokinesis ensues.
source: During exit from mitosis mitotic events are reversed. The mitotic spindle is disassembled, chromosomes decondense and cytokinesis ensues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitotic exit.

claim: Mitotic CDK inactivation brings about exit from mitosis.
source: Mitotic CDK inactivation brings about this transition (Bardin and Amon, 2001; Weiss, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In mammals, CDK inactivation occurs in a single step initiated at the metaphase to anaphase transition.
source: In mammals, CDK inactivation occurs in a single step initiated at the metaphase to anaphase transition.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian cell cycle regulation.

claim: In budding yeast, CDK inactivation is a two-step process.
source: In budding yeast CDK inactivation is a two-step process (reviewed in Sullivan and Morgan, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CDK inhibition begins at the metaphase to anaphase transition when APC/C-Cdc20 targets all S phase cyclins and a fraction of mitotic cyclins for destruction.
source: CDK inhibition begins at the metaphase to anaphase transition when APC/C-Cdc20 targets all S phase cyclins and a fraction of mitotic cyclins for destruction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about budding yeast cell cycle regulation.

claim: APC/C bound to Cdh1 brings about the complete degradation of mitotic cyclins and hence complete mitotic CDK inactivation.
source: Then, in a second step, APC/C bound to a specificity factor related to Cdc20 - Cdh1 - brings about the complete degradation of mitotic cyclins and hence complete mitotic CDK inactivation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about budding yeast cell cycle regulation.

claim: APC/C-Cdh1 is aided in mitotic CDK inactivation by the CDK inhibitor Sic1.
source: APC/C-Cdh1 is aided in mitotic CDK inactivation by the CDK inhibitor Sic1 (Wäsch and Cross, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: APC/C-Cdh1 and Sic1 activity are controlled by the essential protein phosphatase Cdc14.
source: APC/C-Cdh1 and Sic1 activity are controlled by the essential protein phosphatase Cdc14.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cdc14 dephosphorylates Cdh1 and Sic1 thereby activating them.
source: Cdc14 dephosphorylates Cdh1 and Sic1 thereby activating them (Taylor et al., 1997; Jaspersen et al., 1998; Visintin et al., 1998; Zachariae et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: For most of the cell cycle Cdc14 is bound to its inhibitor Cfi1/Net1 in the nucleolus.
source: For most of the cell cycle Cdc14 is bound to its inhibitor Cfi1/Net1 in the nucleolus (Shou et al., 1999; Visintin et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During anaphase Cdc14 dissociates from its inhibitor spreading through the nucleus and cytoplasm to dephosphorylate many proteins including Sic1 and Cdh1.
source: During anaphase the phosphatase dissociates from its inhibitor spreading through the nucleus and cytoplasm to dephosphorylate many proteins including Sic1 and Cdh1.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The FEAR network releases Cdc14 from its inhibitor in the nucleolus upon anaphase entry.
source: The Cdc14 Early Anaphase Release (FEAR) network releases Cdc14 from its inhibitor in the nucleolus upon anaphase entry (Stegmeier et al., 2002; Pereira and Schiebel, 2003; D'Amours et al., 2004; Lavoie et al., 2004; Sullivan et al., 2004; Higuchi and Uhlmann, 2005; Khmelinskii et al., 2007; Woodbury and Morgan, 2007; Roccuzzo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The FEAR network only transiently releases Cdc14 from its inhibitor.
source: The FEAR network only transiently releases Cdc14 from its inhibitor.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cdc14 will return to the nucleolus unless the mitotic exit network (MEN) becomes active.
source: Cdc14 will return to the nucleolus unless the mitotic exit network (MEN) becomes active.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between FEAR and MEN.

claim: Activation of the MEN in late anaphase causes the sustained release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus, resulting in exit from mitosis.
source: Activation of the MEN in late anaphase causes the sustained release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus, resulting in exit from mitosis (Visintin et al., 1998; Visintin et al., 1999; Jaspersen et al., 1999; Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Separase associates with Slk19 which leads to the phosphorylation of the Cdc14 inhibitor Cfi1/Net1 by an unknown mechanism.
source: Separase not only cleaves cohesins, the protease also associates with Slk19 which leads to the phosphorylation of the Cdc14 inhibitor Cfi1/Net1 by an unknown mechanism (Sullivan and Uhlmann, 2003; Yellman and Burke, 2006; Queralt et al., 2006; Wang and Ng, 2006; Azzam et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cfi1/Net1 phosphorylation combined with activation of the FEAR network protein Spo12 leads to Cdc14 release from its inhibitor in the nucleolus.
source: Cfi1/Net1 phosphorylation combined with activation of the FEAR network protein Spo12 then leads to Cdc14 release from its inhibitor in the nucleolus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FEAR network function.

claim: The FEAR network is not essential for exit from mitosis.
source: While Cdc14 released from Cfi1/Net1 by the FEAR network has many roles in facilitating anaphase chromosome segregation (Rock and Amon, 2009), the network is not essential for exit from mitosis (D'Amours et al., 2004; Yoshida et al., 2002; Pereira et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Inactivation of the FEAR network only causes a 20 min delay in exit from mitosis.
source: Inactivation of the FEAR network only causes a 20 min delay in exit from mitosis (Stegmeier et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The MEN is essential.
source: The MEN is essential.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cells lacking MEN function arrest in late anaphase failing to exit from mitosis.
source: Cells lacking MEN function arrest in late anaphase failing to exit from mitosis (Shirayama et al., 1994; Bardin et al., 2000; Geymonat et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The MEN is comprised of the GTPase Tem1, the protein kinases Cdc15 and Dbf2-Mob1, and the signaling scaffold Nud1.
source: The signaling pathway resembles a Ras-like GTPase signal transduction cascade and is comprised of the GTPase Tem1, the protein kinases Cdc15 and Dbf2-Mob1, and the signaling scaffold Nud1 (see Figure 7A for a MEN diagram; reviewed in Stegmeier and Amon, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: MEN components are scaffolded onto spindle pole bodies (SPBs) by Nud1.
source: MEN components are scaffolded onto spindle pole bodies (SPBs), the yeast equivalents of centrosomes, by Nud1 (Valerio-Santiago and Monje-Casas, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Tem1 recruits Cdc15 to SPBs during anaphase.
source: Tem1 recruits Cdc15 to SPBs during anaphase (Visintin and Amon, 2001; Rock and Amon, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cdc15 activates Dbf2-Mob1.
source: Cdc15 then activates Dbf2-Mob1 (Rock et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Active Dbf2-Mob1 promotes the release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus.
source: Active Dbf2-Mob1 promotes the release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus (Mohl et al., 2009; Manzoni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: One function of the MEN is to ensure that sustained Cdc14 activation only occurs when the nucleus moves into the bud during anaphase.
source: One function of the MEN is to ensure that sustained Cdc14 activation only occurs when the nucleus moves into the bud during anaphase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MEN function.

claim: Kin4 activates the Tem1 GTPase activating protein (GAP) complex Bub2-Bfa1 and hence maintains Tem1 in the GDP bound form.
source: Kin4, which activates the Tem1 GTPase activating protein (GAP) complex Bub2-Bfa1 and hence maintains Tem1 in the GDP bound form (Shirayama et al., 1994; Geymonat et al., 2002; Li, 1999; Bloecher et al., 2000) localizes to the mother cell (D'Aquino et al., 2005; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005; Maekawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Kin4 localizes to the mother cell.
source: Kin4, which activates the Tem1 GTPase activating protein (GAP) complex Bub2-Bfa1 and hence maintains Tem1 in the GDP bound form (Shirayama et al., 1994; Geymonat et al., 2002; Li, 1999; Bloecher et al., 2000) localizes to the mother cell (D'Aquino et al., 2005; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005; Maekawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Lte1 inhibits Kin4 and hence activates Tem1.
source: Lte1, which inhibits Kin4 and hence activates Tem1, localizes to the bud (Bertazzi et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Lte1 localizes to the bud.
source: Lte1, which inhibits Kin4 and hence activates Tem1, localizes to the bud (Bertazzi et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Kin4 and Lte1 create a MEN inhibitory zone in the mother cell and a MEN activating zone in the bud, respectively.
source: Thus, Kin4 and Lte1 create a MEN inhibitory zone in the mother cell and a MEN activating zone in the bud, respectively (Figure 1B) (Bardin et al., 2000; Pereira et al., 2000; Chan and Amon, 2010; Falk et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The zone model ensures that the MEN can only be activated when a SPB carrying the MEN GTPase translocates into the bud during anaphase.
source: This setup ensures that the MEN can only be activated when a SPB carrying the MEN GTPase translocates into the bud during anaphase, hence making the MEN responsive to spindle position.
evidence: This is an inference based on the zone model of MEN regulation.

claim: When cells experience a prolonged metaphase arrest the nucleus moves into the bud.
source: It has previously been observed that when cells experience a prolonged metaphase arrest the nucleus moves into the bud (Palmer et al., 1992), yet these cells do not exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Palmer et al., 1992.

claim: Cells arrested in metaphase do not exit from mitosis despite the nucleus moving into the bud.
source: It has previously been observed that when cells experience a prolonged metaphase arrest the nucleus moves into the bud (Palmer et al., 1992), yet these cells do not exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: High mitotic CDK activity prevents MEN activation in metaphase, even when a MEN GTPase-bearing SPB moves into the bud.
source: We show here that high mitotic CDK activity prevents MEN activation in metaphase, even when a MEN GTPase-bearing SPB moves into the bud.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: APC/C-Cdc20 dependent cyclin degradation and activation of Cdc14 by the FEAR network lowers mitotic CDK activity to permit MEN activation upon movement of the SPB into the bud.
source: We further show that APC/C-Cdc20 dependent cyclin degradation and activation of Cdc14 by the FEAR network lowers mitotic CDK activity to permit MEN activation upon movement of the SPB into the bud.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: CDK antagonism of the MEN does not inhibit the MEN GTPase Tem1, but rather causes phosphorylation of downstream components of the MEN, the protein kinases Cdc15 and Mob1-Dbf2.
source: Surprisingly, antagonism by CDKs does not inhibit the MEN GTPase Tem1, but rather causes phosphorylation of downstream components of the MEN, the protein kinases Cdc15 and Mob1-Dbf2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: CDK inhibition of the MEN kinase cascade prevents the feedback loops that would otherwise be initiated upon movement of a MEN GTPase-bearing SPB into the bud.
source: CDK inhibition of the MEN kinase cascade prevents the feedback loops that would otherwise be initiated upon movement of a MEN GTPase-bearing SPB into the bud.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The MEN integrates spatial and temporal signals at different steps of the signaling pathway, demonstrating logical 'AND gate' control of the pathway.
source: Our study shows that the MEN integrates spatial and temporal signals at different steps of the signaling pathway, demonstrating logical 'AND gate' control of the pathway.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Signal integration logic ensures that exit from mitosis only occurs after anaphase entry AND after partitioning of the genetic material between mother and daughter cell.
source: This signal integration logic ensures that exit from mitosis only occurs after anaphase entry AND after partitioning of the genetic material between mother and daughter cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Utilizing multi-point regulation explains how GTPase pathways perform signal integration.
source: Utilizing multi-point regulation explains how GTPase pathways perform signal integration and provides a rationale for why signaling pathways are multi-step processes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Multi-point regulation provides a rationale for why signaling pathways are multi-step processes.
source: Utilizing multi-point regulation explains how GTPase pathways perform signal integration and provides a rationale for why signaling pathways are multi-step processes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: In wild-type cells, Mob1 associates with SPBs when the MEN is activated during anaphase.
source: In wild-type cells, Mob1 associates with SPBs when the MEN is activated during anaphase (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Rock et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and by citation.

claim: Following MEN activation, Cdc14 is released into the cytoplasm.
source: Following MEN activation, Cdc14 is released into the cytoplasm (Figure 1D Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In metaphase-arrested cdc23-1 mutants neither MEN activation nor exit from mitosis occurred.
source: In metaphase-arrested cdc23-1 mutants neither MEN activation nor exit from mitosis occurred.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: SPB movement into the bud caused only weak, inconsistent Mob1 association with SPBs in cdc23-1 mutants.
source: SPB movement into the bud caused only weak, inconsistent Mob1 association with SPBs, Cdc14 was not released from the nucleolus, and cells failed to enter the next cell cycle (Figure 1C–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cdc14 was not released from the nucleolus in cdc23-1 mutants when the SPB moved into the bud.
source: SPB movement into the bud caused only weak, inconsistent Mob1 association with SPBs, Cdc14 was not released from the nucleolus, and cells failed to enter the next cell cycle (Figure 1C–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: cdc23-1 mutant cells failed to enter the next cell cycle when the SPB moved into the bud.
source: SPB movement into the bud caused only weak, inconsistent Mob1 association with SPBs, Cdc14 was not released from the nucleolus, and cells failed to enter the next cell cycle (Figure 1C–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some Mob1 associated weakly with SPBs when the nucleus moved into the bud in cdc23-1 mutants.
source: It is, however, noteworthy that some Mob1 associated weakly with SPBs when the nucleus moved into the bud in cdc23-1 mutants (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The MEN retained at least some ability to respond to spindle position in cdc23-1 mutants.
source: This observation suggests that the MEN retained at least some ability to respond to spindle position.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of weak Mob1 association with SPBs.

claim: MEN activation is suppressed during metaphase.
source: Yet, the low level of Mob1 association with SPBs combined with lack of Cdc14 release from the nucleolus and lack of rebudding indicates that MEN activation is suppressed during metaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Movement of a SPB into the bud causes MEN activation only when it occurs during anaphase.
source: We conclude that movement of a SPB into the bud causes MEN activation only when it occurs during anaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: APC/C-Cdc20 has two essential functions in promoting anaphase onset: cyclin degradation and Securin degradation.
source: Previous work has established that APC/C-Cdc20 has two essential functions in promoting anaphase onset: cyclin degradation and Securin degradation (Figure 1A) (Shirayama et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Cyclin degradation reduces CDK activity during anaphase.
source: Cyclin degradation reduces CDK activity during anaphase.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell cycle biology.

claim: Securin degradation activates the FEAR network.
source: Securin degradation activates the FEAR network and causes cohesin cleavage, which in turn leads to spindle elongation and chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Securin degradation causes cohesin cleavage, which in turn leads to spindle elongation and chromosome segregation.
source: Securin degradation activates the FEAR network and causes cohesin cleavage, which in turn leads to spindle elongation and chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Spindle elongation is not sufficient to activate the MEN in metaphase.
source: Analysis of the cdc23-1, mcd1-1, mad1Δ strain revealed that spindle elongation was not sufficient to activate the MEN in metaphase.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: In cdc23-1, mcd1-1, mad1Δ cells, Mob1 only weakly associated with SPBs.
source: Mob1 only weakly associated with SPBs, Cdc14 was not released from the nucleolus, and cells failed to enter the next cell cycle (Figure 1C–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In cdc23-1, mcd1-1, mad1Δ cells, Cdc14 was not released from the nucleolus.
source: Mob1 only weakly associated with SPBs, Cdc14 was not released from the nucleolus, and cells failed to enter the next cell cycle (Figure 1C–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: cdc23-1, mcd1-1, mad1Δ cells failed to enter the next cell cycle.
source: Mob1 only weakly associated with SPBs, Cdc14 was not released from the nucleolus, and cells failed to enter the next cell cycle (Figure 1C–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In cells depleted for Cdc20, T78 phosphorylation was greatly delayed and diminished, irrespective of whether or not spindle elongation occurred.
source: In cells depleted for Cdc20, T78 phosphorylation was greatly delayed and diminished, irrespective of whether or not spindle elongation occurred (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cells depleted for Cdc20 failed to exit from mitosis as judged by the persistence of anaphase spindles.
source: Furthermore, cells failed to exit from mitosis as judged by the persistence of anaphase spindles in cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Movement of a SPB into the bud is a prerequisite for MEN activation but spindle elongation is not.
source: We conclude that movement of a SPB into the bud is a prerequisite for MEN activation but spindle elongation is not.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Cdc14 release from the nucleolus mediated by the FEAR network is required for the timely activation of the MEN.
source: Previous studies showed that Cdc14 release from the nucleolus mediated by the FEAR network is required for the timely activation of the MEN (Stegmeier et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2002; Pereira et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the absence of FEAR network function MEN activation is delayed by approximately 15–20 min.
source: In the absence of FEAR network function MEN activation is delayed by approximately 15–20 min.
evidence: This is established knowledge confirmed by experimental data in the study.

claim: Inactivation of the FEAR network led to a highly consistent 15 min delay in MEN activation.
source: Inactivation of the FEAR network led to a highly consistent 15 min delay in MEN activation (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpression of a non-degradable form of Pds1 (GAL-PDS1dBΔ) caused a 15 min delay in Nud1T78 phosphorylation and anaphase spindle break-down.
source: Upon release from a pheromone induced G1 arrest, overexpression of a non-degradable form of Pds1 (GAL-PDS1dBΔ) caused a 15 min delay in Nud1T78 phosphorylation and anaphase spindle break-down (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Arrest of cells in metaphase using the microtubule depolymerizing drug nocodazole completely prevented MEN activation and mitotic exit.
source: In contrast, arrest of cells in metaphase using the microtubule depolymerizing drug nocodazole completely prevented MEN activation and mitotic exit.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A similar 15 min delay in Nud1 T78 phosphorylation, Dbf2 kinase activation, and anaphase spindle breakdown was observed in cells harboring a temperature sensitive allele of Separase (esp1-1).
source: A similar 15 min delay in Nud1 T78 phosphorylation, Dbf2 kinase activation, and anaphase spindle breakdown was observed in cells harboring a temperature sensitive allele of Separase (esp1-1) and in two other FEAR network mutants: slk19Δ and spo12Δ bns1Δ (Figure 2C,D; Figure 3A-D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D; Figure 3A-D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A similar 15 min delay in Nud1 T78 phosphorylation, Dbf2 kinase activation, and anaphase spindle breakdown was observed in slk19Δ and spo12Δ bns1Δ mutants.
source: A similar 15 min delay in Nud1 T78 phosphorylation, Dbf2 kinase activation, and anaphase spindle breakdown was observed in cells harboring a temperature sensitive allele of Separase (esp1-1) and in two other FEAR network mutants: slk19Δ and spo12Δ bns1Δ (Figure 2C,D; Figure 3A-D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D; Figure 3A-D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: cdc14-3 cells synchronously released from a pheromone-induced G1 arrest exhibited a 30 min delay in Nud1 T78 phosphorylation and Dbf2 kinase activation.
source: cdc14-3 cells synchronously released from a pheromone-induced G1 arrest exhibited a 30 min delay in Nud1 T78 phosphorylation and Dbf2 kinase activation (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Activation of the FEAR network at the metaphase – anaphase transition contributes to the timely activation of the MEN.
source: We conclude that activation of the FEAR network at the metaphase – anaphase transition contributes to the timely activation of the MEN.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Lack of FEAR network activity in metaphase cannot explain why MEN activation does not occur when a MEN bearing SPB moves into the bud.
source: Lack of FEAR network activity in metaphase cannot explain why MEN activation does not occur when a MEN bearing SPB moves into the bud.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing experimental results from different conditions.

claim: Cdc20-depleted cells neither activated the MEN as judged by a lack of Nud1T78 phosphorylation nor exited mitosis as judged by the persistence of anaphase spindles.
source: Cdc20-depleted cells neither activated the MEN as judged by a lack of Nud1T78 phosphorylation nor exited mitosis as judged by the persistence of anaphase spindles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cells in which FEAR network activity was inhibited by expressing a non-degradable version of Pds1 delayed MEN activation and exit from mitosis by only 20 min.
source: In contrast, cells in which FEAR network activity was inhibited by expressing a non-degradable version of Pds1 delayed MEN activation and exit from mitosis by only 20 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The APC/C-Cdc20 must have an additional role in MEN activation separate from activation of the FEAR network.
source: This result demonstrates that the APC/C-Cdc20 must have an additional role in MEN activation separate from activation of the FEAR network.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing experimental results.

claim: High CDK activity is sufficient to inhibit the MEN.
source: These data demonstrate that high CDK activity is sufficient to inhibit the MEN.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing that overexpression of Clb2dBΔ prevents MEN activation.

claim: Overexpression of Clb2dBΔ prevented MEN activation during anaphase as judged by reduced Mob1 association with SPBs.
source: We found that overexpression of Clb2dBΔ prevented MEN activation during anaphase as judged by reduced Mob1 association with SPBs (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of Clb2dBΔ prevented exit from mitosis as judged by the inability of cells to form a new bud.
source: Exit from mitosis also did not occur as judged by the inability of cells to form a new bud (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Combining overexpression of Clb2dBΔ with the cdc14-3 allele completely abolished Mob1 binding to SPBs.
source: Combining overexpression of Clb2dBΔ with the cdc14-3 allele completely abolished Mob1 binding to SPBs (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: High mitotic CDK activity prevents MEN activation during metaphase.
source: The observation that high mitotic CDK activity in anaphase is sufficient to prevent MEN activation suggested that high mitotic CDK activity prevents MEN activation during metaphase.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: Exit from mitosis depends on both the state of mitotic CDK activity and spindle position.
source: Analysis of Cdc3 localization led to the discovery that exit from mitosis depends on both the state of mitotic CDK activity and spindle position.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: cdc20-1 single mutants arrested in metaphase and did not exit from mitosis as judged by persistent Cdc3 localization at the bud neck.
source: cdc20-1 single mutants arrested in metaphase and did not exit from mitosis as judged by persistent Cdc3 localization at the bud neck (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,D.

claim: Deletion of BUB2 leads to premature MEN activation and, after a significant delay, exit from mitosis in metaphase-arrested cells.
source: Deletion of BUB2 leads to premature MEN activation and, after a significant delay, exit from mitosis in metaphase-arrested cells (reviewed in Gardner and Burke, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In cdc20-1 bub2Δ cells, 78% of cells in which the spindle migrated into the bud exited from mitosis.
source: 78% of cells in which the spindle migrated into the bud exited from mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In cdc20-1 bub2Δ cells, only 36% of cells in which the spindle remained in the mother cell exited mitosis.
source: In mother cells this number was smaller. Only 36% of cells in which the spindle remained in the mother cell exited mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mitotic exit was delayed in both categories of cdc20-1 bub2Δ cells.
source: Interestingly, mitotic exit was delayed in both categories of cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Time from the onset of budding to exit from mitosis took on average 283 min in cdc20-1 bub2Δ cells compared to 86 min in wild-type cells.
source: Time from the onset of budding to exit from mitosis took on average 283 min in cdc20-1 bub2Δ cells compared to 86 min in wild-type cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A MEN inhibitor, presumably CDK activity, prevents MEN activation in a manner that is GAP independent.
source: This delay confirms that a MEN inhibitor, presumably CDK activity, prevents MEN activation in a manner that is GAP independent.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.

claim: Some cdc20-1 bub2Δ cells elongated their spindles prior to cytokinesis.
source: We also noted that some cdc20-1 bub2Δ cells elongated their spindles prior to cytokinesis (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Activation of APC/C-Cdh1 by the MEN not only causes mitotic cyclin degradation but APC/C-Cdh1 can also induce Securin degradation.
source: This observation suggests that activation of APC/C-Cdh1 by the MEN not only causes mitotic cyclin degradation but that APC/C-Cdh1 can also induce Securin degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of spindle elongation in cdc20-1 bub2Δ cells.

claim: Deletion of BUB2 neither caused exit from mitosis nor spindle elongation in cdc23-1 mutants.
source: Consistent with this interpretation is the observation that deletion of BUB2 neither caused exit from mitosis nor spindle elongation in cdc23-1 mutants (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: In cdc23-1 mutants both forms of the APC are inactive and neither mitotic cyclins nor Securin can be degraded.
source: In this mutant both forms of the APC are inactive and neither mitotic cyclins nor Securin can be degraded.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of cdc23-1 mutation.

claim: Inactivating the mitotic cyclin Clb2 using the clb2-VI allele caused mitotic exit in cdc20-1 mutants.
source: Inactivating the mitotic cyclin Clb2 using the clb2-VI allele caused mitotic exit in cdc20-1 mutants (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,D.

claim: Mitotic exit in cdc20-1 clb2-VI mutants only occurred in cells in which the nucleus had moved into the bud during the arrest.
source: Importantly, this exit from mitosis depended on spindle position. Mitotic exit only occurred in cells in which the nucleus had moved into the bud during the arrest.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: cdc20-1 mutants were more likely to undergo mitotic exit than cdc23-1 mutants.
source: cdc20-1 mutants were more likely to undergo mitotic exit than cdc23-1 mutants (Figure 5A), most likely because cdc20-1 mutants can still activate the APC/C-Cdh1, whereas cdc23-1 mutants cannot.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and inference about APC/C function.

claim: Spindle elongation requires mitotic CDK activity.
source: Spindle elongation requires mitotic CDK activity (Rahal and Amon, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The clb2-VI allele likely lowers mitotic CDK activity below the level necessary to accomplish spindle elongation.
source: The clb2-VI allele likely lowers mitotic CDK activity below the level necessary to accomplish this task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that spindle elongation did not occur in clb2-VI mutants.

claim: The MEN kinase Dbf2-Mob1 phosphorylates the NLS of Cdc14, increasing cytoplasmic Cdc14 when the MEN is active.
source: To selectively measure MEN activity we took advantage of the finding that the MEN kinase Dbf2-Mob1 phosphorylates the NLS of Cdc14, increasing cytoplasmic Cdc14 when the MEN is active (Mohl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Release of NLSCdc14 from the nucleus into the cytoplasm depended on MEN activity.
source: Release of NLSCdc14 from the nucleus into the cytoplasm depended on MEN activity, validating this novel MEN assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: In the FEAR network mutant slk19Δ, export of NLSCdc14 from the nucleus was delayed by 20 min.
source: Furthermore, in the FEAR network mutant slk19Δ, export of NLSCdc14 from the nucleus was delayed by 20 min, which is consistent with the 20 min delay in MEN activation observed in slk19Δ mutants. (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: The NLSCdc14 localization assay specifically reports on MEN-dependent control of Cdc14.
source: Most importantly, the analysis of slk19Δ mutants demonstrated that the NLSCdc14 localization assay specifically reports on MEN-dependent control of Cdc14.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: The time difference between release of full-length Cdc14 from the nucleolus and export of the NLSCdc14 from the nucleus was smaller in FEAR network mutants than in wild-type cells.
source: When we compared the release of full-length Cdc14 from the nucleolus with export of the NLSCdc14 from the nucleus we found that the time difference between the two was smaller in FEAR network mutants than in wild-type cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: cdc20-1 single mutants arrested in metaphase did not release NLSCdc14 into the cytoplasm when a SPB translocated into the bud.
source: cdc20-1 single mutants arrested in metaphase did not release NLSCdc14 into the cytoplasm when a SPB translocated into the bud which is consistent with their failure to disassociate Cdc3 from the bud neck and to exit from mitosis (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Deletion of BUB2 caused release of NLSCdc14 into the cytoplasm in metaphase-arrested cells.
source: Deletion of BUB2 caused release of NLSCdc14 into the cytoplasm in metaphase-arrested cells (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: In cdc20-1 clb2-VI mutants in which exit from mitosis occurred, translocation of NLSCdc14 from the nucleus into the cytoplasm was observed.
source: In cdc20-1 clb2-VI mutants in which exit from mitosis occurred (Cdc3 delocalized from the bud neck), we also observed translocation of NLSCdc14 from the nucleus into the cytoplasm (Figure 5E,F), indicating that exit from mitosis in this strain was preceded by MEN activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Spindle position dependent exit from mitosis in cdc20-1 clb2-VI cells required MEN activity.
source: Indeed, we found that spindle position dependent exit from mitosis in cdc20-1 clb2-VI cells required MEN activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that cdc20-1 clb2-VI cdc15-2 triple mutants failed to exit mitosis.

claim: cdc20-1 clb2-VI cdc15-2 triple mutants failed to exit mitosis upon translocation of a SPB into the bud.
source: cdc20-1 clb2-VI cdc15-2 triple mutants failed to exit mitosis upon translocation of a SPB into the bud (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MEN activation requires two signals: (1) movement of a MEN GTPase-bearing SPB into the bud and (2) a lowering of mitotic CDK activity by APC/C-Cdc20 at the onset of anaphase.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that MEN activation requires two signals: (1) movement of a MEN GTPase-bearing SPB into the bud and (2) a lowering of mitotic CDK activity by APC/C-Cdc20 at the onset of anaphase.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: In budding yeast, activation of the DNA damage checkpoint causes cell cycle arrest in metaphase.
source: In budding yeast, activation of the DNA damage checkpoint causes cell cycle arrest in metaphase (Agarwal et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Deletion of BUB2 increased the percentage of cells exiting mitosis in all three DNA damage-inducing conditions.
source: Deletion of BUB2 increased the percentage of cells exiting mitosis in all three DNA damage-inducing conditions (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Combining the clb2-VI allele with the DNA damage-inducing conditions did not cause more cells to exit from mitosis upon movement of the nucleus into the bud.
source: Interestingly, unlike cdc20-1 clb2-VI cells, combining the clb2-VI allele with the DNA damage-inducing conditions did not cause more cells to exit from mitosis upon movement of the nucleus into the bud (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Mechanisms in addition to high mitotic CDK activity prevent MEN activation in cells arrested in metaphase due to DNA damage.
source: This finding indicates that mechanisms in addition to high mitotic CDK activity prevent MEN activation in cells arrested in metaphase due to DNA damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.

claim: DNA damage inhibits the MEN by activating the MEN inhibitory GAP complex, Bub2-Bfa1.
source: Indeed, previous reports have shown that DNA damage inhibits the MEN by activating the MEN inhibitory GAP complex, Bub2-Bfa1 (Valerio-Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Deleting BUB2 allows cdc13-1, cdc9-1 and HU-treated cells to exit from mitosis.
source: Consistently deleting BUB2 allows cdc13-1, cdc9-1 and HU-treated cells to exit from mitosis (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: At least one mechanism in addition to spindle position and high mitotic CDK activity prevents MEN activation in response to DNA damage.
source: We conclude that at least one mechanism in addition to spindle position and high mitotic CDK activity prevents MEN activation in response to DNA damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: The additional inhibitory mechanism preventing MEN activation in response to DNA damage is likely to be activation of the MEN GAP Bub2-Bfa1 by DNA damage.
source: This additional inhibitory mechanism is likely to be activation of the MEN GAP Bub2-Bfa1 by DNA damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and previous literature.

claim: The MEN kinase Cdc15 has 7 CDK phosphorylation sites.
source: Previous work had established that the MEN kinase Cdc15 has 7 CDK phosphorylation sites (Jaspersen and Morgan, 2000); Mob1 has 2 (Valerio-Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mob1 has 2 CDK phosphorylation sites.
source: Previous work had established that the MEN kinase Cdc15 has 7 CDK phosphorylation sites (Jaspersen and Morgan, 2000); Mob1 has 2 (Valerio-Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutation of CDK phosphorylation sites to alanine (cdc15-7A and mob1-2A) prevents their phosphorylation by mitotic CDKs.
source: Mutation of these sites to alanine (cdc15-7A and mob1-2A) prevents their phosphorylation by mitotic CDKs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effect of alanine substitutions.

claim: 21% of cdc15-7A cdc20-1 double mutants were able to exit from mitosis.
source: We found that 21% of cdc15-7A cdc20-1 double mutants were able to exit from mitosis (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Exit from mitosis in cdc15-7A cdc20-1 double mutants depended on movement of a SPB into the bud.
source: Importantly, as seen when lowering mitotic CDK activity, exit from mitosis depended on movement of a SPB into the bud.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 52% of cdc20-1 mob1-2A cells exited mitosis.
source: 52% of cdc20-1 mob1-2A cells exited mitosis (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Exit from mitosis in cdc20-1 mob1-2A cells largely depended on movement of the nucleus into the bud.
source: Exit from mitosis largely depended on movement of the nucleus into the bud. 52% of cells with the spindle in the daughter cell exited mitosis, whereas only 6% of cells exited mitosis in which the spindle remained in the mother cell (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A transient, unobserved excursion of a MEN-bearing SPB into the bud could activate the MEN in a small fraction of cells.
source: We hypothesize that a transient, unobserved excursion of a MEN-bearing SPB into the bud activated the MEN in this small fraction of cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observation that some cells exited mitosis without obvious spindle movement into the bud.

claim: Mitotic exit in cdc20-1 cdc15-7A and cdc20-1 mob1-2A was slow and proceeded by spindle elongation.
source: As observed in cdc20-1 bub2Δ cells, mitotic exit in cdc20-1 cdc15-7A and cdc20-1 mob1-2A was slow and proceeded by spindle elongation (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Exit from mitosis in cdc20-1 mob1-2A cells was accompanied by MEN activation.
source: Importantly, exit from mitosis in cdc20-1 mob1-2A cells was accompanied by MEN activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NLSCdc14 export.

claim: cdc20-1 mob1-2A cells that exited mitosis exported NLSCdc14 from the nucleus into the cytoplasm.
source: cdc20-1 mob1-2A cells that exited mitosis exported NLSCdc14 from the nucleus into the cytoplasm (Figure 6D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Combining the cdc15-7A and mob1-2A allele was additive.
source: Combining the cdc15-7A and mob1-2A allele was additive.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased mitotic exit in the double mutant.

claim: 80% of cdc15-7A mob1-2A cdc20-1 triple mutants exited from mitosis upon movement of the nucleus into the bud during the metaphase arrest.
source: 80% of cdc15-7A mob1-2A cdc20-1 triple mutants exited from mitosis upon movement of the nucleus into the bud during the metaphase arrest and cells exited mitosis more rapidly than either of the double mutants (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Only 15% of cdc15-7A mob1-2A cdc20-1 triple mutant cells where the nucleus remained in the mother cell exited mitosis.
source: In contrast, only 15% of cells where the nucleus remained in the mother cell exited mitosis, presumably due to unobserved, transient excursions by a MEN-bearing SPB into the bud.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CDK activity inhibits the MEN during metaphase by phosphorylating multiple MEN kinases.
source: We conclude that CDK activity inhibits the MEN during metaphase by phosphorylating multiple MEN kinases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: At the onset of anaphase, APC/C-Cdc20 attenuates mitotic CDK activity by (1) targeting a fraction of mitotic cyclins for destruction and (2) inducing FEAR-network mediated release of Cdc14 from its inhibitor in the nucleolus.
source: At the onset of anaphase, APC/C-Cdc20 attenuates mitotic CDK activity by (1) targeting a fraction of mitotic cyclins for destruction and (2) inducing FEAR-network mediated release of Cdc14 from its inhibitor in the nucleolus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and established knowledge.

claim: These two mechanisms restrict MEN activation to anaphase, preventing premature exit from mitosis.
source: These two mechanisms restrict MEN activation to anaphase, preventing premature exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Signal integration in the Mitotic Exit Network occurs through the regulation of multiple signaling elements rather than a central signaling hub.
source: Our results demonstrate that signal integration in the Mitotic Exit Network occurs through the regulation of multiple signaling elements rather than a central signaling hub.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Regulation of the GTPase by spindle position and regulation of the downstream kinase cascade by CDK activity creates a logical 'AND gate'.
source: Regulation of the GTPase by spindle position and regulation of the downstream kinase cascade by CDK activity creates a logical 'AND gate'.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Regulating the MEN signaling cascade in series decreases susceptibility to noise.
source: We propose that regulating the MEN signaling cascade in series decreases susceptibility to noise; a downstream dependence on CDK inactivation insulates the MEN against spindle movement prior to anaphase.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings.

claim: A downstream dependence on CDK inactivation insulates the MEN against spindle movement prior to anaphase.
source: We propose that regulating the MEN signaling cascade in series decreases susceptibility to noise; a downstream dependence on CDK inactivation insulates the MEN against spindle movement prior to anaphase.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings.

claim: Signal integration rather than signal amplification may be the reason for why signal transduction pathways are multi-step processes.
source: Our work also provides an explanation for why signaling pathways are multi-step processes. Signal integration rather than signal amplification may be the reason for why signal transduction pathways are multi-step processes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Positive feedback loops create ultrasensitive, switch-like responses.
source: Positive feedback loops, such as the mutual regulation between Cdc14 and the MEN (Figure 7A,B) as well as double-negative feedback loops, such as exist between CDKs and the MEN (Figure 7A,C), create ultrasensitive, switch-like responses (reviewed in Ferrell and Ha, 2014a; Ferrell and Ha, 2014b; Ferrell and Ha, 2014c).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Double-negative feedback loops create ultrasensitive, switch-like responses.
source: Positive feedback loops, such as the mutual regulation between Cdc14 and the MEN (Figure 7A,B) as well as double-negative feedback loops, such as exist between CDKs and the MEN (Figure 7A,C), create ultrasensitive, switch-like responses (reviewed in Ferrell and Ha, 2014a; Ferrell and Ha, 2014b; Ferrell and Ha, 2014c).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: In MEN regulation ultrasensitivity is isolated to anaphase because of its dependence on APC/C-Cdc20 activity.
source: In MEN regulation this ultrasensitivity is isolated to anaphase because of its dependence on APC/C-Cdc20 activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: APC/C-Cdc20 activates Cdc14 through the FEAR network.
source: APC/C-Cdc20 activates Cdc14 through the FEAR network and decreases mitotic CDK activity through mitotic cyclin degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge confirmed by the study.

claim: APC/C-Cdc20 decreases mitotic CDK activity through mitotic cyclin degradation.
source: APC/C-Cdc20 activates Cdc14 through the FEAR network and decreases mitotic CDK activity through mitotic cyclin degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge confirmed by the study.

claim: APC/C-Cdc20 primes the MEN for robust, anaphase specific signaling.
source: This primes the MEN for robust, anaphase specific signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: When a SPB moves into the bud during metaphase a slight, but appreciable MEN activation occurs.
source: When a SPB moves into the bud during metaphase a slight, but appreciable MEN activation occurs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of weak Mob1 association with SPBs.

claim: Small amounts of Mob1 localize to the SPBs when a SPB moves into the bud during metaphase, yet signaling strength is weak and inconsistent, never leading to release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus.
source: Small amounts of Mob1 localize to the SPBs, yet signaling strength (as judged by Mob1 association with SPBs) is weak and inconsistent, never leading to release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Without the FEAR network, the Cdc14 positive feedback loop is disrupted, slowing MEN activation by 20 min.
source: Without the FEAR network, the Cdc14 positive feedback loop is disrupted, slowing MEN activation by 20 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Without APC/C-Cdc20 degradation of Clb2 and Clb5 at the metaphase – anaphase transition, the double-negative feedback loop between mitotic CDKs and the MEN is too heavily weighted towards CDK activity, preventing MEN activation.
source: Likewise, without APC/C-Cdc20 degradation of Clb2 and Clb5 at the metaphase – anaphase transition, the double-negative feedback loop between mitotic CDKs and the MEN is too heavily weighted towards CDK activity, preventing MEN activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The initial characterization of MEN regulation focused on the MEN GTPase Tem1.
source: The initial characterization of MEN regulation focused on the MEN GTPase Tem1.
evidence: This is a statement about the history of MEN research.

claim: Tem1 was found to make the MEN responsive to spindle position and DNA damage.
source: Tem1 was found to make the MEN responsive to spindle position and DNA damage (Chan and Amon, 2010; Hu et al., 2001; Cooper and Nelson, 2006; Geymonat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: MEN regulatory signals control not just Tem1 but also every subsequent step in the pathway.
source: Our work has revealed that MEN regulatory signals control not just Tem1 but also every subsequent step in the pathway (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: The protein kinase Cdc15 is regulated by the polo-like kinase Cdc5.
source: The protein kinase Cdc15 is regulated by the polo-like kinase Cdc5 (Rock and Amon, 2011) and CDK activity (Jaspersen and Morgan, 2000; Xu et al., 2000; this study).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The protein kinase Cdc15 is regulated by CDK activity.
source: The protein kinase Cdc15 is regulated by the polo-like kinase Cdc5 (Rock and Amon, 2011) and CDK activity (Jaspersen and Morgan, 2000; Xu et al., 2000; this study).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and confirmed by the current study.

claim: The Mob1-Dbf2 kinase is regulated by CDK activity.
source: The Mob1-Dbf2 kinase is regulated by CDK activity (König et al., 2010; this study).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and confirmed by the current study.

claim: The phenotype of the cdc15-7A mob1-2A double mutant indicates that control of the MEN kinases protects cells from spindle movements into the bud such as occur when cells arrest in metaphase for prolonged periods of time.
source: The phenotype of the cdc15-7A mob1-2A double mutant indicates that control of the MEN kinases protects cells from spindle movements into the bud such as occur when cells arrest in metaphase for prolonged periods of time.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.

claim: Movement of the nucleus into the bud during metaphase arrests is not merely a byproduct of cell cycle arrests brought about by mutations in genes critical for anaphase entry.
source: It is worth emphasizing that movement of the nucleus into the bud during metaphase arrests is not merely a byproduct of cell cycle arrests brought about by mutations in genes critical for anaphase entry.
evidence: This is a statement emphasizing the physiological relevance of the phenomenon.

claim: DNA damage or microtubule – kinetochore attachment defects can arrest cells in metaphase for hours.
source: DNA damage or microtubule – kinetochore attachment defects can arrest cells in metaphase for hours.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Live cell analyses show that wild-type cells arrest in metaphase at an appreciable frequency presumably due to light-induced DNA damage.
source: Indeed, our live cell analyses show that wild-type cells arrest in metaphase at an appreciable frequency presumably due to light-induced DNA damage.
evidence: This is an observation from the study with a speculative explanation.

claim: In 67% of metaphase-arrested wild-type cells the spindle moves in the bud.
source: In 67% of these arrested cells the spindle moves in the bud.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Even transient excursions of the spindle into the bud during metaphase could lead to inappropriate Tem1 activation.
source: Our data further suggest that even transient excursions of the spindle into the bud during metaphase could lead to inappropriate Tem1 activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.

claim: 15% of cdc15-7A mob1-2A double mutants exited mitosis during the metaphase arrest without obvious and hence inferred transient movement of the nucleus into the bud.
source: 15% of cdc15-7A mob1-2A double mutants exited mitosis during the metaphase arrest without obvious and hence inferred transient movement of the nucleus into the bud.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of the MEN kinase cascade by mitotic CDKs prevents inappropriate mitotic exit prior to anaphase.
source: In either case our findings indicate that inhibition of the MEN kinase cascade by mitotic CDKs prevents inappropriate mitotic exit prior to anaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: It is possible that mitotic CDKs regulate additional MEN components.
source: Although the phenotype of the cdc15-7A mob1-2A double mutant was similar to that of the clb2-VI mutant, it is possible that mitotic CDKs regulate additional MEN components.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging limitations of the study.

claim: Mass spectrometry studies have detected phosphorylation consistent with modification by CDKs on many MEN components and regulators including Bfa1, Cdc5, Cdc14, Lte1, Nud1, Tem1, and Dbf2.
source: Mass spectrometry studies have detected phosphorylation consistent with modification by CDKs on many MEN components and regulators including Bfa1, Cdc5, Cdc14, Lte1, Nud1, Tem1, and Dbf2 (Ubersax et al., 2003; Holt et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.
